\chapter{Things You Ask For}
\label{ch:ta-things-you-ask-for}
\hlchaptermodality{44}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five everyday things I might ask somebody for in Tamil, and say which of them Tamil has held all along and which arrived from elsewhere.}

Complete TA-C44-book and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[paḻam]{\ta{பழம்} (paḻam) — a fruit}

\label{lesson:TA-C44-fruit}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{makaḷ} mean, and what did \emph{kuṭumbam} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{பழம்}}
\textbf{\ta{பழம்}} (\emph{paḻam}) — \textquotedblleft{}a fruit\textquotedblright{}.

Underneath it is a root about ripening. Proto-Dravidian \textbf{*paḻ}, 'to ripen, to grow old', handed this family both a fruit and an age, and Tamil kept the pair close enough to hear: \emph{paḻaiya}, the \textquotedblleft{}old\textquotedblright{} from the run of describing words, is that same root wearing a different ending. Ripe and old are one idea seen twice.

Malayalam says \ml{പഴം}, very nearly the identical word — the ordinary state of affairs between the two closest sisters. Telugu went to \te{పండు} (\emph{paṇḍu}) and Kannada to \ka{ಹಣ್ಣು} (\emph{haṇṇu}), and the Kannada form has lost its opening \emph{p-} to a shift Tamil sat out entirely.

The \ta{ழ} in the middle is the letter this book has already spent a writing lesson on, the one only these two sisters still write.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five things you might ask somebody for.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{paḻam}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{paḻam}, then \emph{tayavu seytu paḻam koṭuṅgaḷ} — \textquotedblleft{}please give a fruit\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{பழம்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a fruit\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tuṇi]{\ta{துணி} (tuṇi) — cloth}

\label{lesson:TA-C44-cloth}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{paḻam} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{துணி}}
\textbf{\ta{துணி}} (\emph{tuṇi}) — \textquotedblleft{}cloth\textquotedblright{}.

One shape, two jobs. \emph{tuṇi} is the cloth you wear or wipe your hands on, and \emph{tuṇi} is also 'to dare, to resolve'. Nothing joins them but sound, and the sentence around them settles which is meant — the ordinary way a language carries two words in one skin.

Malayalam keeps \ml{തുണി} unchanged. Telugu and Kannada reach for something else here, so this is one of the places where the two closest sisters agree and the other two go their own way.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: something to eat and something to wear.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tuṇi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{paḻam}, then \emph{tuṇi}, so the two sit together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{துணி} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}cloth\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[viḷakku]{\ta{விளக்கு} (viḷakku) — a lamp}

\label{lesson:TA-C44-lamp}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{tuṇi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{விளக்கு}}
\textbf{\ta{விளக்கு}} (\emph{viḷakku}) — \textquotedblleft{}a lamp\textquotedblright{}.

It stands on \emph{viḷaṅgu}, 'to shine, to be clear', so the lamp is named for what it does rather than for what it is made of.

The same stem gives \emph{viḷakkam}, 'clarity', and \emph{viḷakku} on its own can mean 'to make something plain'. A lamp and an explanation are the same word in Tamil, which is a better picture of teaching than most languages get for free.

A Tamil house lights one at dusk, at the doorway, and the word turns up wherever that habit does.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, and the third one shines.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{viḷakku}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{tuṇi}, then \emph{viḷakku}, and hear the doubled letter in the second
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{விளக்கு} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a lamp\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[uppu]{\ta{உப்பு} (uppu) — salt}

\label{lesson:TA-C44-salt}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{viḷakku} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{உப்பு}}
\textbf{\ta{உப்பு}} (\emph{uppu}) — \textquotedblleft{}salt\textquotedblright{}.

Proto-Dravidian \textbf{*upp-}, and none of the four sisters did much to it: Malayalam \ml{ഉപ്പ്}, Telugu \te{ఉప్పు}, Kannada \ka{ಉಪ್ಪು}. Set them beside \ta{உப்பு} and you are looking at one word in four hands.

A word that stable is usually a word nobody could do without. Salt is also how Tamil talks about savour in general — food with no \emph{uppu} in it is food with nothing in it at all.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and this one has not changed in a very long time.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{uppu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{viḷakku}, then \emph{uppu}, and let the second one stop short
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{உப்பு} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}salt\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[puttakam]{\ta{புத்தகம்} (puttakam) — a book}

\label{lesson:TA-C44-book}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{uppu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{புத்தகம்}}
\textbf{\ta{புத்தகம்}} (\emph{puttakam}) — \textquotedblleft{}a book\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{pustaka}, taken in whole, with the \emph{-am} Tamil puts on the end of such arrivals — the same \emph{-am} already sitting on \emph{kuṭumbam}. Malayalam \ml{പുസ്തകം}, Telugu \te{పుస్తకం} and Kannada \ka{ಪುಸ್ತಕ} are the same borrowing, so the four agree here for a different reason than they agree about salt: not descent, but a shared debt.

Tamil kept its own word alongside. \ta{நூல்} (\emph{nūl}) is a thread, and thread is what bound palm leaves into a book before there was paper; the same \emph{nūl} still names a written work. The borrowed word and the inherited one divide the job between them rather than fighting over it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five, and the run is closed: a fruit, cloth, a lamp, salt, a book.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{puttakam}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{paḻam}, \emph{tuṇi}, \emph{viḷakku}, \emph{uppu}, \emph{puttakam}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{புத்தகம்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a book\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
